title: From Phone Box to Push Alert: How Classifieds Got This Complicated

know: The steps by which advertising a thing for sale moved from a sign on the thing itself to today's listing platform, and the concept each step introduced: the listing as a promise about a thing the reader cannot see; freshness and the race to reach the seller first; the contact; the publisher's rules, its price per line and its categories; the specialist title for one kind of goods, with professional sellers and the same few questions asked of every ad; the free listing the seller publishes alone; search, filters and an order of results that the site decides and can sell; the feed sent by a dealer's or agent's software; the saved search and the alert on a phone, and the message inside the platform; payment, checks on who people are and rules set by law; and groups of marketplaces that share one platform.

For each step, both sides of it: what it made possible that could not happen before (a buyer who never walks past the house, a buyer in the next town, a buyer comparing every car in the region, a seller who pays nothing, a buyer who finds one item among millions, a dealer who lists two hundred cars without typing, a buyer who hears of a new ad within minutes, a buyer who can pay a stranger in another city), and what it cost (one more copy of the ad that has to be kept true, one more party, one more delay or one more stranger to trust).
believe: Each step was a good bargain for seller and buyer alike, and no step was ever removed, so today's complexity is the sum of those bargains, not a design mistake.
Given those steps, the failure patterns of the next page are what one should expect, not signs of careless engineering.
can_do: Given a term from a later chapter (listing, contact, category, insertion fee, attribute, moderation, ranking, paid visibility, feed, saved search, alert, buyer protection), say which step of the walk introduced it and what limit it answered.
Given a failure pattern's name, say which step makes it possible.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader new to classifieds can say, for a concept the page introduces, which step brought it in and what limit of the earlier way of advertising it answered.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why is a newspaper ad already out of date on the morning it appears, and which earlier way of advertising did not have that problem?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The ad is printed once and runs until the edition ends, but the thing can be sold to the first caller within an hour, after which every later caller is answering an ad that is no longer true; the paper cannot take it back. The page names the speed at which an ad stops being true, and the race to reach the seller first, as freshness and the contact. A sign on the thing itself had no such problem: when the thing was sold, the sign went with it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can connect a failure pattern to the step that makes it possible.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: a bike sold on Monday still appears in an alert on Tuesday morning. Which steps made that possible, and which named pattern is it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: It starts with the card and the newspaper ad, which outlive the sale; it becomes a recurring failure once the website lets the seller alone remove the ad and once the ad exists in several copies (search, alerts) that each learn of the sale at their own time. The page names it Ghost Inventory.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every dated fact on the page has a source the style guide accepts, the page says once that it is a simplified account that follows the ideas, generalizations about how people used classifieds are marked as common practice or illustration, and it attributes no motives to companies.
Every term is given in plain words before it is named, and no step uses a concept a later step introduces.
A reader can say, for a step of the walk, what it made possible for the seller and for the buyer as well as what it cost.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: when a dealer's software sends its whole stock to a portal every night, who gains what, and who risks what?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The dealer lists every car without typing and keeps the ads in step with the lot; the buyer sees the dealer's whole stock with the same details for every car. The portal now publishes what another company's system says, when that system sends it: a cut-short file can remove cars that are still for sale, a removal arrives only with the next file, and the same flat sent by three agencies appears three times.

thesis.question: How did selling a second-hand thing to a stranger, once done with a sign on the thing itself, come to need so many systems, copies of the ad and checks on the people at either end?
thesis.claim: Classifieds became complicated one good bargain at a time: each new way of advertising (the card in a shop window, the newspaper column, the specialist magazine, the free website, search and a sold order of results, the dealer's feed, the alert on a phone, payment and checks on the platform) let a seller reach buyers who could not see the thing and let a buyer reach it sooner, and paid for it with one more copy of the ad that had to be kept true and one more stranger to trust; none was retired, so a listing today must be true at once in every copy, for buyers and sellers either of whom may be lying.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a classifieds site is a simple thing (a table of ads and a search box) made complicated by old code, acquisitions or over-engineering, so that a clean rebuild would make it simple again.
thesis.so_what: A reader who sees each step as a bargain that both sides wanted stops looking for the rebuild that removes the copies and the checks, expects a failure wherever one copy of an ad learns the truth later than another or a stranger can act before anyone checks, and reads the fifteen patterns of the next page as the price of what the steps made possible.
thesis.how_why: A sign on the thing is true as long as the thing is there, and only passers-by can read it. Every later step lets more buyers find more things (the neighbour, the town that reads the paper, the region that buys the car magazine, anyone online, anyone searching, anyone with an alert on a phone) by moving the ad further from the thing, so the ad becomes a promise that can stop being true before its readers know. Each step added a copy (the card, the printed column, the page, the search index, the feed, the alert) that learns of a sale at its own time, and a reader or a seller the other side has never met; the race to call first, which began at the phone box, is still the race the platform has to make fair and safe. The dates on the page are a small set of sourced anchors, and the account is a simplification that follows the ideas.

supporting_claims.claim: A sign on the thing cannot outlive the sale and needs no trust in a description; the first step away from it, a card in a shop window, already has what every later system has: a listing that promises something the reader cannot see, a copy that can outlive the sale, someone who decides which ads may be shown, and strangers on both sides who may be lying.

Each later way of advertising (the newspaper column, the specialist magazine, the website, search and a sold order, the feed, the alert on a phone) made a sale possible that could not happen before, to the gain of seller and buyer alike, by moving the ad further from the thing or bringing the buyer to it sooner.

Each addition brought its own way to go wrong: a new copy of the ad that learns of a sale late, a new party whose rules or systems the seller depends on, or a new stranger who can act before anyone checks.

No step was ever removed, so a listing today lives in all of them at once, with payment, identity checks, law, group platforms and models on top, and the failures the next page names are the price of what the steps made possible.

role.contribution: Explains, before the failure patterns are named, where the copies of an ad, the race to be first and the strangers on both sides came from, what each step made possible and what it cost, and introduces in plain words the vocabulary Part I and later parts then teach properly.

additional_patterns.applies_to: sign to today: the steps are in the order the ideas accumulated, which is roughly the order of the dates; the sign, the card and the column are undated common practice and come first because the later steps build on them
inside each step: the limit, the addition and its name, what it made possible, what it cost, the answer to the running question

flow.rationale: Each step uses only concepts that earlier steps introduced: the listing as a promise apart from the thing before the column that prints it for a town; the column's categories, price per line and race to call before the magazine that adds photos, attributes and professional sellers; the self-published listing and its lifecycle before search, which needs the magazine's attributes as data and copies the listings into an index; the index and the order of results before the feed, whose removals have to reach that index; and the contact, the index and the copy before the alert, which is a copy that races to a buyer. Payment, identity checks and group platforms come last because each rests on the messaging and the scale that the earlier steps created. The magazine comes before the website even though both coexisted for decades, because attributes and professional sellers are needed to explain search and feeds; the page says 'by then' where the dates overlap.

hook.content: On a Saturday morning, an illustration of common practice, a reader buys the local paper as early as she can, rings a cheap bike in the small ads and runs to a telephone box with coins; if the line is busy, someone else got there first, and the ad keeps offering the sold bike to the town until the next edition. In 2027 the book's fictional Rotterdam bike gets its first message thirteen minutes after it is listed and is still offered in 214 alert e-mails the morning after it was sold.

bridge.from_reader_world: Everyone has seen a card in a shop window, small ads in a paper and an alert on a phone.
bridge.to_topic: The phone box and the push alert are the same race run by different machinery; between and before them lie other ways of advertising, each of which let someone buy or sell who could not before.

thesis_statement.text: Classifieds became complicated one good bargain at a time: each new way of advertising (the card in a shop window, the newspaper column, the specialist magazine, the free website, search and a sold order of results, the dealer's feed, the alert on a phone, payment and checks on the platform) let a seller reach buyers who could not see the thing and let a buyer reach it sooner, and paid for it with one more copy of the ad that had to be kept true and one more stranger to trust; none was retired, so a listing today must be true at once in every copy, for buyers and sellers either of whom may be lying.

promises.promise: The walk starts at a sign on the thing itself and its first complication, a card in a shop window.
It continues through the newspaper column and the specialist magazine.
Then the classifieds website, search and the order of results, the dealer's feed and the phone in the pocket.
It ends on today's platform, shown in the book's fictional case, with one question answered at every step: is what the ad says still true, and who finds out first?

sections.heading: The Sign on the Thing: The Ad Cannot Outlive the Sale
sections.controlling_idea: A sign taped to the thing itself is the simplest ad: the ad, the thing and the seller are in one place, so the ad cannot outlive the sale, but only passers-by can read it.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the baseline in which the ad cannot go stale and needs no trust in a description, and names the three conditions whose failure starts every later step.

flow.rationale: The sign is the baseline, so it has no limit to answer: one sale comes first, then why its ad cannot go stale, then the three conditions that fail in every later step, then the first answer to the running question.

transition_in.carries_over: The route and the question announced in the introduction.
transition_in.introduces: The first step: the simplest way to advertise a thing for sale, as the baseline.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A bike leaning on a garden fence with a price on a card taped to it is sold to a passer-by who sees it, tries it, knocks and pays.

evidence.what: An illustration of common practice: a bike by a garden gate with a for-sale card; a passer-by tries it and pays.
evidence.shows: Gives the simplest form of advertising, which every reader has met.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ad and the thing are in one place: the buyer sees what she buys, the seller is at the door, and when the bike is sold the sign goes with it.

transition_in.carries_over: A sale where the sign is on the thing.
transition_in.introduces: Why that ad cannot go stale and needs no trust in a description.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: It is that simple only under three conditions (the buyer walks past, the thing is where the sign is, the seller is next to it), and each later step begins where one of them did not hold.

evidence.what: Figure: the bike on the fence with its sign, a passer-by, the seller at the door.
evidence.shows: The scene every later figure adds to.

transition_in.carries_over: An ad that cannot outlive the sale.
transition_in.introduces: The three conditions that make it possible, and the announcement that later steps start where they fail.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The sign is true as long as it hangs on the thing, and whoever walks past finds out first.

transition_in.carries_over: The sign on the thing and its three conditions.
transition_in.introduces: The step's answer to the running question: is what the ad says still true, and who finds out first?

sections.heading: The Card in the Shop Window: An Ad Away From the Thing
sections.controlling_idea: Moving the ad off the thing, onto a card in a shop window, already creates what every later system has: a listing that is a promise about a thing the reader cannot see, a copy that can outlive the sale, someone who decides which ads may be shown, and strangers on both sides who may be lying.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the first ad apart from the thing, with no technology at all, already needs trust, rules and a way to take the ad down.

flow.rationale: The limit of the earlier way of advertising comes first, then what was added and its name, then what it made possible for both sides, then what it cost, then the answer to the running question. The term cannot be named before the reader has seen the need it answers, and the cost cannot be weighed before the gain.

transition_in.carries_over: The sign reaches only those who walk past.
transition_in.introduces: The oldest way around that: the same words on a card where many people look.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A seller pays a corner shop to put a card in its window; the card describes a thing the reader cannot see, at an address nearby, and the book calls such a public, time-bound offer about a thing a listing, a promise that the thing exists, is as described and is still for sale.

evidence.what: Illustration of common practice: a card for a pram in a shop window among a dozen others.
evidence.shows: Shows the first listing apart from its thing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The seller reaches everyone who uses the shop, and the buyer sees a dozen offers in one place.

transition_in.carries_over: A listing in a shop window.
transition_in.introduces: What it made possible for each side.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The card can stay up after the sale, can describe the thing better than it is, and brings a stranger to the seller's door, so the shopkeeper starts to decide which cards go up and turns away those that look like trouble: the plainest form of a marketplace's rules and of moderation, and of the trust each side needs in the other.

evidence.what: Figure: a card still in the window while the pram is wheeled away elsewhere; the shopkeeper sorts cards.
evidence.shows: Gain and price together.

transition_in.carries_over: What the card made possible.
transition_in.introduces: What it cost: staleness, a description that can lie, strangers on both sides, rules and moderation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The card is true until the sale and stays up for days after; whoever reads it first and knocks finds out, the rest at the door.

transition_in.carries_over: The card's gain and its cost.
transition_in.introduces: The step's answer to the running question: is what the ad says still true, and who finds out first?

sections.heading: The Newspaper Column: The Race to the Phone Box
sections.controlling_idea: The newspaper's classified columns reach a whole town each morning, under the publisher's rules, categories and price per line, and start the race to reach the seller first, in which the printed ad is out of date the moment the first caller gets through.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the publisher, categories, the insertion fee, the network effect, the contact and freshness in the scene a newcomer can picture.

flow.rationale: The limit of the earlier way of advertising comes first, then what was added and its name, then what it made possible for both sides, then what it cost, then the answer to the running question. The term cannot be named before the reader has seen the need it answers, and the cost cannot be weighed before the gain.

transition_in.carries_over: A card reaches one street.
transition_in.introduces: A paper that reaches a whole town every morning.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Newspapers commonly sold small ads grouped under headings in narrow columns; a business whose job ends when a reader contacts the seller is what the book calls classifieds, and the headings are categories, chosen by the paper with the order of ads under them.

transition_in.carries_over: A card reaches one street.
transition_in.introduces: The newspaper column, classifieds and categories.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The paper is a publisher that sets the rules and charges by the line or by the word; a charge to publish an ad is what the book calls an insertion fee.

transition_in.carries_over: Classifieds and categories.
transition_in.introduces: Who runs the column and how it is paid for.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The seller reaches a whole town in a day, the buyer sees every offer in the town over breakfast, and the paper with the most ads draws the most readers, which draws more ads: a network effect.

transition_in.carries_over: The column, its rules and its price.
transition_in.introduces: What it made possible for each side, and why one paper wins a town.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because the best offers go fast, a buyer commonly gets the paper as early as possible, rings an ad and runs to a telephone box with coins to call the seller before anyone else; the call is the contact, and how fast it comes is what the book measures as time to first contact.

evidence.what: Illustration of common practice: a buyer with an early paper, a ringed ad and coins, at a telephone box.
evidence.shows: The author's opening scene, the heart of the page.

evidence.what: Figure: a buyer with an open newspaper in a telephone box, coins on the shelf, a ringed ad.
evidence.shows: The race to be first.

transition_in.carries_over: Every offer in the town on one page.
transition_in.introduces: The race those offers start: the paper, the ringed ad and the phone box.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The printed ad is out of date the moment the first caller gets through, yet runs until the next edition; how fast a sold thing disappears from where buyers see it is freshness, and the race is unfair to the late reader while caller and seller, strangers at a distance, can each deceive the other.

transition_in.carries_over: The race to call first.
transition_in.introduces: What the column cost: an ad that cannot be taken back, freshness, and deception at a distance.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ad is true until the first call gets through but printed as true until the next edition; the reader who got the paper first and reached a phone first finds out first, the rest from an engaged tone.

transition_in.carries_over: The race and the stale ad.
transition_in.introduces: The step's answer to the running question: is what the ad says still true, and who finds out first?

sections.heading: The Specialist Magazine: Photos, Dealers and the Same Few Questions
sections.controlling_idea: A magazine for one kind of goods, such as cars, gathers a region's ads with photos and the same few facts for each, mostly from dealers and agents, so buyers can compare, at the price of ads printed days before they are read and photos that may not show the thing.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the vertical, the professional seller, attributes and the photo as the first media.

flow.rationale: The limit of the earlier way of advertising comes first, then what was added and its name, then what it made possible for both sides, then what it cost, then the answer to the running question. The term cannot be named before the reader has seen the need it answers, and the cost cannot be weighed before the gain.

transition_in.carries_over: A line of text in a town paper.
transition_in.introduces: What a buyer of a car needs before she calls: a photo and the same facts for every car.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Specialist titles for one kind of goods gathered a region's ads, commonly with a photo each; Auto Trader's own history dates Thames Valley Trader to 1977, and a marketplace for one kind of goods is what the book calls a vertical.

evidence.shows: Dates the step without claiming a first.

transition_in.carries_over: A line of text in a town paper.
transition_in.introduces: The specialist magazine and the vertical.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every ad answers the same questions (make, model, year, mileage, price), which the book calls attributes, the photo is the first media, and most ads come from professional sellers who advertise every week and pay for it.

transition_in.carries_over: The magazine for one kind of goods.
transition_in.introduces: What it added: attributes, photos and professional sellers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The buyer compares every car in the region on one page before she calls, and dealers sell a lot's worth of cars across a region.

transition_in.carries_over: Photos, attributes and dealers.
transition_in.introduces: What it made possible for each side.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A weekly deadline makes the ad days old before it is read, a photo can show another or a better car, and the same car can appear in two magazines.

evidence.shows: Gain and price together.

transition_in.introduces: What it cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ad was true when written days before print and its photo may not be of this car; the reader in the region who gets the magazine first finds out first.

transition_in.carries_over: The magazine's ads, photos and dealers.
transition_in.introduces: The step's answer to the running question: is what the ad says still true, and who finds out first?

sections.heading: The Classifieds Website: Free, Instant and Unchecked
sections.controlling_idea: On a website the seller publishes the ad herself, at once and commonly for free, and can remove it at any time, which lets anyone sell to anyone at any hour, at the price of ads nobody checked first, ads nobody removes, and counts of ads that grow faster than sales.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the self-published listing, its lifecycle, moderation after the fact and the difference between counting ads and counting matches.

flow.rationale: The limit of the earlier way of advertising comes first, then what was added and its name, then what it made possible for both sides, then what it cost, then the answer to the running question. The term cannot be named before the reader has seen the need it answers, and the cost cannot be weighed before the gain.

transition_in.carries_over: Print waits for its deadline and charges by the line.
transition_in.introduces: A page that can be changed at any time and costs almost nothing per ad.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A web page can change at any time and costs almost nothing per ad; craigslist's own history dates its start to e-mailed notices in early 1995 that software later posted to a website, Auto Trader dates its first website to 1996, and eBay's 2004 announcement says Marktplaats, founded in 1999, had more than a million listings at any given time.

transition_in.carries_over: Web pages that change at any time.
transition_in.introduces: What was added: self-publishing, free listings and the listing lifecycle.

transition_in.introduces: The step's answer to the running question: is what the ad says still true, and who finds out first?

sections.heading: Search and Filters: The Site Decides the Order
sections.controlling_idea: When a city has thousands of ads, the site adds a search box and filters, which need categories and attributes as data and a copy of every ad in a search index, and decides the order of results, which it can sell, at the price of a copy that learns of a sale late, a tree and fields fixed in the site, and an order buyers can no longer read.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces search, the search index, attributes as required data, the category tree, ranking and paid visibility.

flow.rationale: The limit of the earlier way of advertising comes first, then what was added and its name, then what it made possible for both sides, then what it cost, then the answer to the running question. The term cannot be named before the reader has seen the need it answers, and the cost cannot be weighed before the gain.

transition_in.carries_over: Every ad in the country on one site.
transition_in.introduces: Too many ads to read, and the tools that find one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Too many ads to read leads to a search box and filters, which work only if every ad has a category from a tree and the same named fields, and which read from a copy of the ads, the search index.

transition_in.carries_over: Every ad in the country on one site.
transition_in.introduces: Search, filters, the category tree and the search index.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The site decides the order of results (newest, nearest or most relevant), which the book calls ranking, and because the order is the site's it can sell places in it, a bump or a top slot: paid visibility.

transition_in.carries_over: Search and filters.
transition_in.introduces: The order of results and its sale.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The buyer finds the one bike among thousands in seconds, the seller of a good bike is found by the buyer who wants exactly that, and a seller in a hurry can pay to be seen first.

transition_in.carries_over: Search, filters and an order.
transition_in.introduces: What it made possible for each side.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The index is a copy that learns of a sale late and can be mistaken for the record, the tree and fields are built into the site so a new kind of thing needs a change to it and sellers type the rest as free text, and every paid place pushes down a free one so buyers cannot tell the best result from the paid one.

evidence.shows: Gain and price together.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ad is true in its own record and in the index only as of the last update; the site's record finds out first, then the index, then the buyer.

sections.heading: Feeds: The Dealer's Software Writes the Ad
sections.controlling_idea: Dealers and agents commonly let their own software send their stock to the portals as a feed, which lists every car without typing, at the price of a portal that publishes what another company's system says, when it says it.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the feed and its contract, and the duplicate that arrives from several professional sellers.

flow.rationale: The limit of the earlier way of advertising comes first, then what was added and its name, then what it made possible for both sides, then what it cost, then the answer to the running question. The term cannot be named before the reader has seen the need it answers, and the cost cannot be weighed before the gain.

transition_in.carries_over: Sellers who type their ads into a site.

sections.heading: The Phone in the Pocket: The Race Becomes a Notification
sections.controlling_idea: With the site in the buyer's pocket, a saved search sends an alert within minutes of a new ad and the call moves into the platform as a message, so the race to the phone box becomes a push notification, at the price of alerts built from copies and a channel where fraud closes.

advances_thesis.how: Introduces the saved search, the alert, in-platform messaging and the lead, and plants the fraud that closes in the conversation.

flow.rationale: The limit of the earlier way of advertising comes first, then what was added and its name, then what it made possible for both sides, then what it cost, then the answer to the running question. The term cannot be named before the reader has seen the need it answers, and the cost cannot be weighed before the gain.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Once apps sit on phones (Apple's App Store opened on 10 July 2008), a buyer can save a search and be told when a new ad matches, a saved search and its alert, and can message the seller inside the app; for a dealer each message is a lead.

sections.heading: Today: Payment, Proof and One Platform for Many Marketplaces
sections.controlling_idea: Today's platform adds payment and buyer protection, checks on who people are, rules set by law, groups that share one platform across brands and countries, and models that decide, and Veldmark's Rotterdam bike shows every step at once.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the present keeps every earlier step and adds money, identity, law, group platforms and models on top, and brings in the fictional case only here.

flow.rationale: The limit of the earlier way of advertising comes first, then what was added and its name, then what it made possible for both sides, then what it cost, then the answer to the running question. conclusion.heading: What the Steps Add Up To
conclusion.synthesis: Read together, the steps show one movement no single step shows: each moved the ad further from the thing and put more strangers between seller and buyer, and the answer to 'is it still true, and who finds out first?' grew from 'yes, whoever walks past' to one record and a dozen copies that learn at different times.
conclusion.so_what: The steps answer limits that still exist and each bought trade both sides wanted, so no rebuild removes the copies and the checks; a builder should expect a failure wherever one copy learns the truth later than another or a stranger can act before anyone checks.

callback.to: The phone box and the Rotterdam bike.
callback.how: The race to call first is still there: thirteen minutes from listing to first message, and an alert e-mail thirteen hours after the sale.

takeaway.content: The failure patterns of the next page are the price of what these steps made possible, not signs of careless engineering.

hand_off.carries_over: The steps of the previous page: each way of advertising moved the ad further from the thing, added a copy that learns of a sale at its own time and a stranger to trust, and none was removed; together with the introduction's liquidity-machine claim and its short list of pattern names.
hand_off.introduces: What those steps make possible: each of the fifteen patterns unpacked, with quote, warning signs, mechanism, cost, a Veldmark illustration, the remedy direction and the chapters that address it; then the chains between them.

Teaching any mechanism properly: each concept gets plain words, its name and a link.

open_questions: No primary source was read for the newspaper step (prices per line, the order of ads, the morning race) or for the card in a shop window; both are written as common practice and illustration, without dates.

decision_log.decision: Nine steps: sign on the thing, card in a shop window, newspaper column, specialist magazine, classifieds website, search and the order of results, feeds, the phone in the pocket, today. Payment and buyer protection, identity checks, regulation, group platforms and models are joined in the last step, as what the present adds.
rejected: A separate step for payment and buyer protection (ten steps; its concepts are part of today's platform in the book).
Teletext or telephone ad lines (country-specific; no concept the tally needs).
Starting at the newspaper (too complex a first step; the author asked for a simpler start).
A separate step for portfolio groups (chapter 3 owns that history).

decision_log.decision: The running question is 'Is what the ad says still true, and who finds out first?', answered in a closing paragraph of every step that begins with the question in bold.
rejected: 'Who can be trusted?' (trust appears in the costs; truth and timing are what most patterns turn on).

decision_log.decision: Each of the fifteen pattern names appears once in the tally: Moderation as an Afterthought, Ghost Inventory and Vanity Liquidity at the website; The Category Straitjacket, The Attribute Junkyard, Search as System of Record and Multiplier Creep at search; Feed Roulette and Seeing Double at feeds; Fast Mail for Fraudsters at the phone; The Copy-Paste Country, Deal-Shaped Architecture, The Forced Fit, Billing by Guesswork and Set-and-Forget AI at today.
rejected: Listing a pattern at every step that can produce it (Ghost Inventory would appear five times).

decision_log.decision: Anchor dates, each from a page fetched on 18 November 2026: 1977, 1988, 1996 and 2013 (Auto Trader Group's history page), early 1995 (craigslist's history page), 1999 and 2004 (eBay's 2004 press release on Marktplaats, SEC exhibit), 2000-2007 (NYU Stern on Seamans and Zhu, 2013), 2008 (Apple Newsroom), 2017 and 2019 (Adevinta Annual Report 2023), 2021 (Adevinta press release), 2024 (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065), 2025 (UK Finance Annual Fraud Report 2026).
